theme: Deliver me from evil men; with my voice I cry to the LORD
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 140 and Psalm 142. The first asks God to protect from violent and slanderous men. The second is David’s prayer in the cave. Notice how each ends with a statement of confidence.
settingTheScene: Psalm 140 is a psalm of David asking for deliverance from violent men. Psalm 142 is a Maskil of David, when he was in the cave, which refers to his flight from Saul in 1 Samuel 22 or 24. They conclude this series of psalms on injustice. In the first, evil men plot. In the second, the psalmist cries out from a place where no one cares for him.
observation: “Deliver me, O LORD, from evil men; preserve me from violent men” (140:1).
“They make their tongue sharp as a serpent’s, and under their lips is the venom of asps” (140:3).
“I say to the LORD, You are my God; give ear to the voice of my pleas for mercy, O LORD!” (140:6).
“O LORD, my Lord, the strength of my salvation, you have covered my head in the day of battle” (140:7).
“I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and will execute justice for the needy” (140:12).
“With my voice I cry out to the LORD; with my voice I plead for mercy to the LORD” (142:1).
“When my spirit faints within me, you know my way!” (142:3).
“I cry to you, O LORD; I say, You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living” (142:5).
interpretation:
In Psalm 140, the danger is both physical and verbal. The enemies “plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually.” Their words are sharp as a snake’s. The psalmist feels hunted: they have hidden a trap for him and spread a net. His response is not to fight but to pray. “I say to the LORD, You are my God.” It is the simplest declaration of faith. In the middle of danger, he claims his relationship with the LORD.

A phrase deserves attention: “You have covered my head in the day of battle.” In war, the head is the most vulnerable. God has been his helmet. It is a vivid expression of divine protection. And at the end, the psalmist declares confidence: “I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted.” He knows. His faith rests not on seeing but on God’s character.

Psalm 142 brings us to the cave. David is alone, hunted, and desperate. He prays aloud: “With my voice I cry out.” There is no pretense. He pours out his complaint and tells his trouble before God. The line that stands out is verse 4: “Look to the right and see: there is none who takes notice of me; no refuge remains to me; no one cares for my soul.” It is the cry of utter loneliness. But the next verse is the turn: “I cry to you, O LORD; I say, You are my refuge, my portion in the land of the living.”

When no human refuge remains, the psalmist declares that God is his refuge. “You are my portion,” he says, as the Levites who had no land received the LORD as their inheritance. Everything has been stripped from David, and he discovers that God is enough.

The psalm ends with a hope: “Bring me out of prison, that I may give thanks to your name! The righteous will surround me, for you will deal bountifully with me.” The cave will not be the last word. He will again be among God’s people.
connection: Jesus, in Gethsemane and on the cross, was alone, forsaken by his disciples (Matthew 26:56). Yet he said, “I am not alone, for the Father is with me” (John 16:32). Hebrews 13:5-6 promises, “I will never leave you nor forsake you,” so we can say, “The Lord is my helper.” Ephesians 6:17 says to take the helmet of salvation. 2 Timothy 4:16-17 echoes Paul’s abandonment and the Lord’s strengthening.
application:
If you feel that no one cares for your soul, pray Psalm 142:5 aloud: “You are my refuge, my portion.”

Pray verse 140:7 and ask God to cover your head in the day of battle.

Look for someone who is alone and take notice of them.
prayerPrompts: Tell God you are his and he is yours.
Ask him to deliver you from evil and to be your refuge.
Tell him what faints within you.
